## Critical point 1: Managing generated HTML files

### Problem encountered

Each group member worked on a separate .qmd file and needed to render it as HTML to check the code, explanations, and graphs without rendering the entire main document every time.

However, rendering individual sections generated additional HTML files and folders that appeared as changes in GitHub Desktop. We did not want to manually exclude these files every time we made a commit because they were only generated for preview purposes.

### Solution implemented

We updated the .gitignore file to automatically ignore the generated HTML files and temporary Quarto folders.

**Quarto generated files**
*_files/
.quarto/
sections/*.html

This allowed each member to preview their work independently without adding unnecessary generated files to the Git repository, keeping commits cleaner and easier to manage.

## Critical point 2: Reusing functions and libraries across sections

### Problem encountered

Our assignment was divided into separate .qmd files, but later sections needed to reuse functions and variables from earlier sections. Although the files were included in the correct order in the main Quarto document, we encountered errors when trying to reuse this code.

For example, Section 4 needed the original signal (s) and time vector (t) from Section 3, but these variables were not available because the latest Section 3 changes had not yet been merged into our working branch.

After updating the branch, we also encountered a FileNotFoundError because the load_qmd_code() function was looking for earlier .qmd files in the wrong directory.

### Solution implemented

We updated our working branch with the latest completed sections from main so that the required functions and variables were available.

We then corrected the file paths in load_qmd_code() by adding sections/ before the filenames, allowing Python to locate and execute the earlier files.

We also added shared library imports to the main Quarto document so they were available throughout the assignment.

These changes allowed us to reuse our teammates' functions instead of rewriting them and ensured that the sections worked together when rendering the full document.


## Critical point 3

### Problem encountered

While organizing our GitHub repository, we renamed the branch for Section 1. However, this caused the original pull request to close automatically, even though the section was not yet merged into main.

This created confusion because the completed work was still available, but the original pull request could no longer be used to review and merge it.

### Solution implemented

We created a new pull request using the correct branch and checked that it contained the intended changes before merging.

This showed us the importance of keeping branch names consistent and avoiding unnecessary branch renaming while pull requests are open, especially when several group members are contributing to the same repository.
